entries.clue: Secret police heads launch fierce attack  and pay dearly? (6,3)

indicatorNotes.heads: The head of a word is the letter it starts with, and the plural asks the same of each of the two words standing before it.

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of those two words
to lash out is to launch a sudden violent attack on somebody

annotation.surface: The top brass of the secret police ordering a violent raid.
annotation.walkthrough: Heads reads as the bosses giving the order and asks for two initials instead. The two halves of the answer are hidden by the clue's own phrasing, since launch fierce attack is a definition of the back half rather than an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: To splash out is to spend far more than you needed to, so you do pay dearly — in cash, not in the suffering the phrase usually threatens.

entries.clue: Prince is making an appearance? Should get jail! (6)

blocks.note: pr is the short form of the title, the one an envelope uses
the little word taken straight off the page, letter for letter
a performer who is on has gone out in front of the audience

annotation.surface: A prince showing his face in public, and where he ought to be sent instead.
annotation.walkthrough: The title shrinks to two letters while the verb beside it is spelt out in full, which is the opposite of the weighting the sentence gives them. Private Eye has one particular prince in mind.
annotation.definitionFit: A prison is the building a court sends you to, which is what jail names in the plainer word.

entries.clue: Go-ahead from America on lump debts (9)

blocks.note: am is the usual short form of the country's name
a lump of something is a bit of it, broken off
an IOU is the scribbled note that says money is owed, and here there is more than one

annotation.surface: American approval for settling a pile of debt.
annotation.walkthrough: Go-ahead is the green light in the sentence and an adjective in the answer, the sort applied to a firm that keeps pushing forward. Three ordinary chunks in a row is the whole mechanism.
annotation.definitionFit: A go-ahead company is one with big plans and the drive to chase them, which is ambitious in its enterprising rather than its grasping sense.

entries.clue: Swinger guy's wrapped in glitzy top (5)

indicatorNotes.wrapped: To wrap something is to go round the outside of it, so the word named before it closes over what comes after.
indicatorNotes.top: In a down entry the top of a word is the letter printed highest, which is the one it begins with.

blocks.note: a guy is a he, the pronoun standing in for the man
the little word taken off the page as the two letters it is spelt with
the letter that word begins on

annotation.surface: A partner-swapper done up inside a flashy sparkly top.
annotation.walkthrough: Wrapped in reads as one instruction and would put the guy inside something; in fact he does the wrapping and the word in is two of the letters he closes over. Glitzy contributes a single letter, not a shuffle.
annotation.definitionFit: A hinge is the fitting a door or a gate swings on, so swinger names it by the one thing it exists to do.

entries.clue: New York institution on Don's strip (7)

blocks.note: the United Nations, whose headquarters stand on the East River in Manhattan
to don a coat is to dress in it

annotation.surface: The United Nations pronouncing on a mafia boss's football kit.
annotation.walkthrough: Don is a verb here rather than a crime boss or an Oxford tutor, and it carries a capital only because the setter wants the mafia in view. Strip does the same double duty, a kit in the sentence and an action in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: To undress is to take your clothes off, which is what strip means used as a verb of a person.

entries.clue: Material: shag (5)

blocks.note: the everyday word for cloth, or for whatever a thing is made of
British slang for having sex, wanted here as a verb

annotation.surface: A label on a roll of shagpile in a carpet showroom.
annotation.walkthrough: Shag names a long-piled carpet as well as the act, which is what keeps the two words reading as one label. The second half is the vulgar verb the Eye can never leave alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Stuff is the plain word for fabric or substance, and to stuff somebody is the same coarse verb that shag is, so both halves land on it.

entries.clue: Boost to French city   no English! (5)

indicatorNotes.no: No means there is none of it present, so the letter named after it is taken out of what has just been built.

blocks.note: the preposition taken straight off the page, letter for letter
Nice is the big city of the French Riviera
e is the standard short form of English, and it is the letter that departs

annotation.surface: A French city given a lift now that the English have cleared off.
annotation.walkthrough: English is a single letter in crossword shorthand rather than a nationality being thrown out, and the exclamation mark is there to keep the joke about tourists alive. Boost is a noun: the pick-me-up, not the shove.
annotation.definitionFit: A tonic is anything that picks you up and leaves you brighter than it found you, which is a boost to the spirits.

entries.clue: Box decomposed  keep at bay (5,3)

blocks.note: to box is to fight with gloves on, the ring sense rather than the container
food that has gone off has begun to decompose

annotation.surface: A wooden box found rotted right through.
annotation.walkthrough: Decomposed sits exactly where an anagram indicator would sit and shuffles nothing at all: it is a plain synonym for a short word. Box is the ring sense, not the object the sentence shows you.
annotation.definitionFit: To fight something off is to beat it back and hold it away from you, which is what keeping it at bay describes.

entries.clue: Managed a bonk, right, given large double support (8)

indicatorNotes.Managed: Something managed has been arranged by somebody else's hand, so these letters do not stay as they were printed.
indicatorNotes.double: To double a thing is to have two of it, so the single letter just named is written out twice.

blocks.note: a bonk is British slang for sex, and these are five of the six letters the anagram works on
r is the standard short form of right, and it is the sixth letter to be shuffled
l is the short form of large, here written twice and joined on unshuffled

annotation.surface: Somebody who managed a bonk with the benefit of some sizeable support.
annotation.walkthrough: Managed reads as an achievement in the sentence and is the instruction to rearrange in the parse. Double asks for the large one twice over rather than describing anything in the picture.
annotation.definitionFit: To bankroll a venture is to put up the money that keeps it going, which is support in its purely financial sense.

entries.clue: Celebrated striker, well-endowed guy (3,3)

blocks.note: well-endowed is the coy way of saying generously sized, which the Eye means anatomically
an ordinary man's first name, supplied without any signal that a name is wanted

annotation.surface: A famous centre-forward who is also a remarkably well-hung bloke.
annotation.walkthrough: Striker sends you straight to the football pitch, and the thing that strikes here is a bell — one that hangs in the Elizabeth Tower and lends its name to the whole clock in ordinary speech.
annotation.definitionFit: Big Ben is the great bell at Westminster that strikes the hours, and few objects in Britain are more celebrated.

entries.clue: Duke gets drunk, in a rage  it gets rid of the effluent (8)

annotation.definition: it gets rid of the effluent

indicatorNotes.gets drunk: Somebody who gets drunk stops keeping things in any order, and letters in no order are not the ones you were given.

blocks.note: d is the standard short form of duke, and it is joined on unshuffled
the seven letters the anagram works on, gathered from all three words

annotation.surface: A drunken duke in a towering temper.
annotation.walkthrough: The duke shrinks to a single letter and the rage is not his mood but seven letters to rearrange, so the whole sentence collapses into wordplay. Effluent is the polite word for sewage.
annotation.definitionFit: Drainage is the system of pipes and channels laid to carry waste water away from a building or a field.

entries.clue: Congestion of guts and cheek (10)

blocks.note: bottle is British slang for nerve — losing your bottle is losing your courage
neck is the brass-faced sort of cheek, as in the neck of the man

annotation.surface: Somebody made up of equal parts courage and sheer nerve.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are body parts in the sentence and slang for boldness in the parse, which is why the clue reads as a compliment. The answer is a narrowing that jams traffic, and it is a body part too.
annotation.definitionFit: A bottleneck is the pinch point where a road or a process narrows and everything backs up behind it, which is congestion by its cause.

entries.clue: see 22ac.
Gutted creationists accepting massive flash would produce this (6)

annotation.definition: Gutted creationists accepting massive flash would produce this

indicatorNotes.Gutted: Something gutted has had its insides taken out, leaving only the letters standing at the two ends.
indicatorNotes.accepting: What a word accepts it takes inside itself, so the letters named after it go within the ones already found.

blocks.note: the two letters at the ends of that word, everything between them thrown away
os is outsize, the clothing label's word for huge
a flash is a moment, and mo is the short form — back in a mo

annotation.surface: Devastated creationists coming round to the Big Bang.
annotation.walkthrough: Gutted means devastated of the creationists in the sentence and means hollowed out in the parse, and both readings are live at once. Creationists put the world at a few thousand years old, which is what a massive flash would overturn.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a creationist who let the Big Bang in would end up with precisely the expanding universe the answer names.

entries.clue: City's source of marble, not crappy concrete (8)

indicatorNotes.source of: The source of a word is where it starts, so only its opening letter is wanted.
indicatorNotes.crappy: A crappy job is one done badly, and letters done badly do not come out in the order they went in.

blocks.note: the letter that word begins with
the three letters the anagram works on
concrete evidence is real evidence, the sense of solid rather than of cement

annotation.surface: A city's marble quarry, and the shoddy concrete it will not touch.
annotation.walkthrough: Concrete is the building material throughout the sentence and an adjective meaning solid in the parse, which is the clue's one real decision. Crappy shuffles the tiny word beside it rather than passing judgement on the mix.
annotation.definitionFit: Montreal is the largest city in Quebec and the second largest in Canada, offered here under the plain category it belongs to.

entries.clue: United rotten, so matchless (3-3)

blocks.note: people who are united are at one about something
meat that has gone off is rotten

annotation.surface: United playing rotten football and still with nobody to match them.
annotation.walkthrough: United is the state of agreeing rather than the football club the capital invites you to see, and rotten is about food rather than form. The hyphen in the enumeration marks where the two halves meet.
annotation.definitionFit: A one-off happens once and is never repeated, so nothing can be set beside it — which is what matchless claims.

entries.clue: I swear I'll use one! (9)

blocks.note: read as the speaker giving their solemn word, which is the promise the sentence makes
read the other way, to swear is to curse, and one is whatever a curser reaches for

annotation.surface: Somebody promising on their honour to make use of something.
annotation.walkthrough: Swear carries the oath and the four-letter word at the same time, and the clue is built so that the first sense conceals the second. Nothing here comes apart into letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An expletive is a swear word, so the moment anyone swears they are using one — which is exactly the claim the clue makes about itself.

entries.clue: Expose Republicans involved in police operation storm (8)

indicatorNotes.involved in: Someone involved in an operation is caught up inside it, so the letters named first go within the ones named after.

blocks.note: to out somebody is to expose a secret they were keeping
a bust is a raid, the word every crime drama uses for a drugs swoop
r is the letter the party goes by on any American ballot

annotation.surface: A drugs raid with Republicans caught up in it.
annotation.walkthrough: Storm is the last word of the sentence and the definition on its own, meaning a sudden flare of temper rather than weather. Out and bust are both short slang terms, which is why so long an answer comes out of so few pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: An outburst is anger arriving all at once and spending itself, which is what a storm of temper describes.

entries.clue: Navigator: "Treacherous sound hard ahead!" (6)

indicatorNotes.Treacherous: Something treacherous will not stay as it presents itself, and letters that will not stay put do not keep their printed order.
indicatorNotes.ahead: Ahead means out in front, so the letter it describes goes before everything else rather than after it.

blocks.note: h is the standard short form of hard, the grade stamped on a pencil
five of the six letters at work, the word being a channel of water in the sentence

annotation.surface: A navigator yelling a warning about rough water coming up.
annotation.walkthrough: Ahead is doing real work rather than filling out the shout: it says the single letter goes in front. Henry Hudson sailed for the Muscovy Company and then the Dutch, and both a river and a bay carry his name.
annotation.definitionFit: Henry Hudson was the English sea captain who charted the river and the bay now named after him, so navigator offers him as one example of the trade.

entries.clue: Performing sit-up, squashing large bloomers (6)

indicatorNotes.Performing: A move being performed is being gone through rather than left written down, so these letters are put through new positions.
indicatorNotes.squashing: What is squashed is pressed in among other things, so the letter named after it joins the ones already being moved.

blocks.note: five of the six letters at work, the hyphen counting for nothing
l is the short form of large, the sixth letter pressed in among the rest

annotation.surface: Doing sit-ups on top of a large pair of bloomers.
annotation.walkthrough: Bloomers are voluminous knickers in the sentence and things that flower in the answer, which is the whole joke. Large is one letter joining the shuffle, not a comment on anybody's underwear.
annotation.definitionFit: Tulips are the spring bulbs every park plants in blocks, so bloomers names them by the one thing a flower does.

entries.clue: Pissed, needing a small measure  "Make it fast!" (7)

blocks.note: tight is one of the many British words for drunk
the en is the printer's unit of width, half of an em

annotation.surface: A drunk who needs one more small one, and an order barked at him.
annotation.walkthrough: Pissed is British for drunk rather than American for furious, which is what makes the small measure read as a drink. Fast here means firmly fixed, the sense that survives in hold fast and stuck fast.
annotation.definitionFit: To tighten a rope or a bolt is to make it fast — fast in its old sense of held firm, not of quick.

entries.clue: Broadcast cap? Who gives a toss? (2,4)

blocks.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it by hand across a field
a cap is a hat, the soft kind with a peak

annotation.surface: A cap being given away on the radio.
annotation.walkthrough: Broadcast meant scattering seed for centuries before it meant radio, and the older sense is the one the clue wants. Giving a toss is British for caring at all, so the question expects no answer.
annotation.definitionFit: So what? is the shrug you give when something does not matter to you in the least, which is what who gives a toss? asks out loud.

entries.clue: (13ac.) Kind-hearted whip or man-eater? (3)

blocks.note: big-hearted and kind-hearted say the same thing, so one of those first words stands in for the other
the cat-o'-nine-tails, the knotted whip the Royal Navy once flogged men with

annotation.surface: A soft-hearted parliamentary whip, or something that eats people.
annotation.walkthrough: Whip is the Commons enforcer in the sentence and a naval lash in the parse, the pairing that makes the clue read as an insult. The answer runs on into a second entry, so three letters are nowhere near enough.
annotation.definitionFit: The big cats are the lions, tigers and leopards, the family that now and then kills a person — which is what the question mark concedes.

entries.clue: Repulsive amount of money given to TV host (5)

blocks.note: a g is a grand, a thousand pounds in the slang of every crime drama
Jonathan Ross has fronted British chat shows since the eighties

annotation.surface: A wad of cash quietly slipped to a television presenter.
annotation.walkthrough: Repulsive reads as part of the sum being handed over and is the definition standing on its own. A surname arrives with no signal that a name is wanted, which is the usual price of a short answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Something gross is disgusting enough to turn the stomach, which is what repulsive says of it in the politer register.

entries.clue: (& 29ac.) Tories regret fitness fiasco  it reveals MPs' involvements outside parliament (8,2)

annotation.definition: it reveals MPs' involvements outside parliament

indicatorNotes.fiasco: A fiasco is a thing that has gone thoroughly wrong, and letters that have gone wrong are not left standing as printed.

blocks.note: the nineteen letters the anagram works on, gathered from all three words

annotation.surface: The Conservatives ruing a health-and-fitness scheme that went badly wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: Every letter comes from the three words before the break, which is why the answer has to run across two entries to hold them. Private Eye's interest is the outside earnings MPs declare, and how late they declare them.
annotation.definitionFit: The Register of Members' Financial Interests is the published Commons list of MPs' second jobs, gifts and shareholdings, so it reveals exactly what the definition describes.

entries.clue: Bastard involved in marketing fur (5)

indicatorNotes.involved in: Somebody involved in a business is mixed up inside it, so the letter named first goes within the word named after.

blocks.note: a sale is what marketing is for, and the letters part after the second
b is the letter the word is cut down to when it is too rude to print

annotation.surface: A nasty piece of work mixed up in the fur trade.
annotation.walkthrough: Bastard shrinks to its bleeped initial, which is the step the sentence hides by making him a person rather than a letter. The animal is a small Siberian marten whose pelt has always been the expensive one.
annotation.definitionFit: Sable is the dark glossy pelt of that marten, the most prized of the trade's furs, so fur names it by its commodity.

entries.clue: Cocksure rag or crap TV presenter (8)

indicatorNotes.crap: Something crap has been done badly, and letters done badly do not come out in the order they went in.

blocks.note: five of the eight letters at work, rag being the Eye's word for a cheap newspaper
Ant McPartlin, the shorter half of the Geordie television double act Ant and Dec

annotation.surface: A cocksure little newspaper, or a hopeless television presenter.
annotation.walkthrough: Crap looks like a verdict on the presenter and is the instruction to rearrange, and the Eye is perfectly happy for it to read both ways. The word or is fodder rather than a choice being offered.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone arrogant carries themselves as though they could not possibly be wrong, which is what cocksure says with more swagger.

entries.clue: Blast Badenoch's debut  "no heavyweight" (6)

indicatorNotes.debut: A debut is a first appearance, so what is wanted is the letter the name appears with first.

blocks.note: the letter the Conservative leader's surname starts on
anybody who is no heavyweight is a light one

annotation.surface: Kemi Badenoch's first outing, written off as the work of no heavyweight.
annotation.walkthrough: Kemi Badenoch has led the Conservatives since 2024, and only her initial is wanted. No heavyweight is a boxing division in the sentence and a plain adjective in the parse.
annotation.definitionFit: To blight a crop or a person's hopes is to wither them where they stand, which is what blast means used of the same thing.

entries.clue: Street criminal has hidden drugs? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is one hoard rather than a number of drugs, and the question mark concedes that the definition names what is in it instead of the thing itself.

indicatorNotes.criminal: A criminal is bent, and letters bent out of shape are not left standing in the order they were printed.

blocks.note: st is the short form of street on any road sign, and it is joined on unshuffled
the three letters the anagram works on

annotation.surface: A street villain caught with the drugs put away somewhere.
annotation.walkthrough: Hidden belongs to the definition and gives no instruction at all, which is the trap: nothing in this clue is concealed inside anything else. Criminal is the word that does the shuffling, in its sense of bent.
annotation.definitionFit: A stash is a hoard kept out of sight, and drugs are what the word is reached for most often to describe.
